messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 54-year-old forester, had spent thirty years reading the forest—its wind patterns, the lean of trees, the hidden rot in a trunk. But one afternoon, a sudden gust twisted the crown of a towering pine he was felling, sending the trunk off its intended fall. His partner, a younger man named Eric, was standing thirty feet away, in what should have been safe ground. The butt of the tree swung sideways and caught Eric across both legs, shattering his femur and crushing his knee. David heard the crack over the chainsaw's whine, saw Eric's face go white before he even hit the ground. In the weeks that followed, David could not stop replaying that moment. When he closed his eyes, his arms would rise involuntarily, as if still gripping the saw's handles—a bodily reenactment that left him trembling with rage at himself and a grief that felt bottomless. What frightened him most was the conviction that had taken root: there was something about him that had made it happen, some intrinsic fault that had waited decades to show itself. He was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, and he could not rely on himself to keep others safe.

The triggers were everywhere. Physical pain in his lower back—an old injury from years of carrying heavy gear—would flare when he bent to load equipment, and in that instant he would feel his body lock into the same position as when the tree had twisted. He would see a man in a blue hard hat like Eric's and the memory would crash over him, bringing the rage and the grief fresh. Physical proximity to the site of the accident, even just driving the logging road that passed near it, made his chest tighten and his eyes dart to the treetops. These reminders did more than bring the past to mind; they convinced him anew that he was fundamentally broken. Each time he drove past that stretch of forest, the thought came: *You did this. You can't trust yourself.* And each time, a new layer of threat settled over him. Even at home, in his own living room, he could not relax. He had begun watching people—strangers in the grocery store parking lot, coworkers at the equipment shed—for signs of danger, certain that they could see his failure written on him. A stranger approaching to ask for directions made his pulse spike; he felt threatened by ordinary encounters because, he reasoned, if something went wrong it would be his fault again.

The memory itself acted as a trigger. When the image of Eric's crumpled legs surfaced, his body would reenact the position—arms up, knees braced—which then sent a fresh jolt of physical pain through his back, creating a new somatic trigger that looped back into threat. The more he watched others for signs of harm, the more he noticed small lapses in safety protocols among his crew, which fed his belief that he could no longer do the job he had loved. In time, David began avoiding any situation that required him to lead a team. He took only solo inventory tasks, staying away from the felling areas. His wife noticed he had stopped laughing, stopped reaching for her at night. She found him standing at the kitchen window at 2 a.m., scanning the dark yard. When she asked what he was looking for, he could not say. What he felt was a constant readiness, a coiled alertness from which no place felt safe.

What finally brought David to the clinic was a morning in the tool shed when a new hire—a young man with a blue hard hat—stepped too close to him. David had shouted, backed away, and then stood shaking under the weight of his own rage and shame. He was afraid he would hurt someone again, not physically but by being so unraveled that he made a catastrophic mistake. He desperately wanted to believe he could go back to the forest without this constant terror, but he could not imagine what that would feel like.

violation_explanations: No paragraph shows that the patient's sense of threat leads to intrusive memories of the trauma; memories are triggered by external cues, not by the threat state itself.

No paragraph shows that the patient's sense of threat creates new triggers; triggers are independently present (physical pain, blue hard hat, proximity to site) and are not described as caused by threat.
